objectives: Identify the major noble grape varieties and describe their canonical flavour profiles and home regions.
Distinguish still, sparkling, fortified, and dessert wine styles and explain the production method that defines each.
Explain the méthode traditionnelle for Champagne production and the role of single-varietal versus blended wines in fine wine.

slides.title: The noble varieties — red and white archetypes
slides.body:
Ampelography — the science of identifying grape varieties — recognises over **10 000** named *Vitis vinifera* cultivars. Of these, a small cohort of **noble varieties** dominate the fine-wine world, each with a canonical home region, a characteristic flavour profile, and a defined set of structural parameters (acidity, tannin, body, alcohol). DNA profiling by **Carole Meredith** and colleagues at UC Davis (notably the 1997 paper establishing that Cabernet Sauvignon is a natural cross of **Cabernet Franc × Sauvignon Blanc**) has revealed a web of parentage relationships that links many varieties.

**Major red noble varieties**:

- **Cabernet Sauvignon**: thin-skinned, late-ripening, high tannin, high acidity, blackcurrant / cassis / cedar / mint / graphite. Home: **Médoc and Graves** (Bordeaux, France). Thrives in warm climates: **Napa Valley** (California), **Coonawarra** (Australia, on terra rossa soil over limestone). Ages magnificently; the backbone of the **Bordeaux blend**.
- **Merlot**: thicker-skinned, earlier-ripening, lower tannin, plum / chocolate / mocha / bay leaf. The dominant variety of **Pomerol** and **Saint-Émilion** (Right Bank Bordeaux); **Château Pétrus** (Right Bank, clay soils) is almost entirely Merlot.
- **Pinot Noir**: thin-skinned, low tannin, high acid, notoriously difficult to grow, cherry / raspberry / earthiness / forest floor. The sole red variety of **Côte d'Or Burgundy**; also central to **Champagne** (as a base wine), **Oregon's Willamette Valley**, **Central Otago** (New Zealand), and **Martinborough**.
- **Syrah / Shiraz**: thick-skinned, full body, high tannin, violet / blackberry / smoked meat / white pepper (as Syrah, cool climate Northern Rhône: **Hermitage**, **Côte-Rôtie**); jammy plum / eucalyptus / dark chocolate (as Shiraz, warm climate: **Barossa Valley**, **McLaren Vale** Australia). DNA evidence confirms they are the same variety.
- **Nebbiolo**: the grape of **Barolo** and **Barbaresco** (Piedmont, Italy). High acid, very high tannin, moderate colour (pale garnet), rose / tar / dried cherry / truffle. The **Langhe** hills south of **Alba** are its heartland. **Bruno Giacosa** and **Angelo Gaja** are two of its most celebrated modern interpreters.
- **Sangiovese**: the backbone of **Chianti Classico**, **Brunello di Montalcino** (as the clone Brunello), and **Vino Nobile di Montepulciano** — all Tuscany. High acid, medium-high tannin, cherry / dried herbs / leather / iron. **Antinori**'s *Tignanello* (1971 vintage, first commercial release) was one of the first wines to blend Sangiovese with Cabernet Sauvignon, creating the 'Super Tuscan' category.

**Major white noble varieties**:

- **Chardonnay**: the world's most planted noble white variety. Neutral pulp — it expresses terroir and winemaking rather than intrinsic aroma. Unoaked: green apple / lemon / mineral (Chablis, northern Burgundy). Barrel-fermented and aged: peach / butter / vanilla / toast (Meursault, Puligny-Montrachet, oaked California). The dominant grape in **Champagne** blends and the sole grape of **Blanc de Blancs**.
- **Sauvignon Blanc**: aromatic, high acid, green / herbaceous / grapefruit / passionfruit. Benchmarks: **Sancerre** and **Pouilly-Fumé** (Loire, France); **Marlborough** (New Zealand, where **Montana Wines**, now Brancott Estate, planted the first commercial Sauvignon Blanc in 1973). Rarely oaked except in **Pessac-Léognan** (Bordeaux), where it blends with Sémillon in whites like **Château Haut-Brion Blanc**.
- **Riesling**: the great noble white of Germany, Alsace, and Austria. Naturally high acid, variable sweetness, petrol / citrus / slate / apricot. Ranges from bone-dry **Rheingau Erstes Gewächs** to TBA sweetness (see Oechsle in Lesson 2). Virtually never oaked. Ages magnificently — a 1990 Mosel Auslese at peak is one of the world's great wine experiences.
- **Chenin Blanc**: the Loire Valley's chameleon. Grown at **Vouvray** (sparkling and still), **Savennières** (austere dry), **Quarts de Chaume** and **Bonnezeaux** (sweet). Extreme acid and longevity; honey / beeswax / quince / straw. In South Africa (often called Steen) it is the most planted variety.

slides.title: Wine styles — still, sparkling, fortified, and dessert
slides.body:
Wine's extraordinary stylistic range is the product of four fundamental variables: **fermentation completion** (dry vs sweet), **carbonation** (still vs sparkling), **fortification** (addition of neutral spirit), and **concentration** (drying, freezing, or botrytis-affected grapes). Understanding these axes lets a sommelier navigate any wine list and any cellar.

**Still wines**: fermentation runs to completion (dry) or is arrested (sweet). **Residual sugar (RS)** is the defining metric: < 4 g/L = bone dry; 4–12 g/L = off-dry; 12–45 g/L = medium-sweet; > 45 g/L = sweet. Still wines comprise the vast majority of global wine production.

**Sparkling wines** contain dissolved CO₂ sufficient to produce effervescence (typically 5–6 atmospheres of pressure in a Champagne bottle). The **méthode traditionnelle** (also called **méthode champenoise**, *metodo classico* in Italy, *Cava* in Spain, *Sekt* on German labels using this method) produces the finest bubbles through a **second fermentation in the bottle**. The process:
1. **Base wine (vin de base)**: still, dry, high-acid wine (typically 10–11% ABV) assembled from multiple parcels and often multiple vintages (for non-vintage Champagne).
2. **Liqueur de tirage**: a mixture of wine, sugar, and yeast added to each bottle before **crown capping**.
3. **Prise de mousse (second fermentation)**: the yeast consumes the added sugar in the sealed bottle, producing CO₂ (which dissolves under pressure) and alcohol, raising ABV by ~1.2–1.5%.
4. **Lees aging (sur lattes)**: bottles lie horizontal on their sides for a minimum of **15 months** for non-vintage Champagne (NV) and **36 months** for vintage Champagne, per AOC regulations. Lees contact generates **autolysis** — breakdown of dead yeast cells produces the characteristic brioche, biscuit, and creamy characters.
5. **Riddling (remuage)**: gradual rotation and tilting of bottles (originally by hand by a *remueur*; now mostly by **gyropalette**, a mechanical cage invented in the 1970s) to collect yeast sediment in the neck.
6. **Disgorgement (dégorgement)**: the neck is frozen in brine, the crown cap removed, and the frozen yeast plug expelled by bottle pressure.
7. **Dosage (liqueur d'expédition)**: a mixture of reserve wine and sugar added to adjust final sweetness: **Brut Nature** (0–3 g/L RS), **Extra Brut** (0–6 g/L), **Brut** (< 12 g/L), **Extra Dry** (12–17 g/L), **Demi-Sec** (32–50 g/L).

The **Dom Pérignon myth**: the Benedictine monk **Dom Pierre Pérignon** (1638–1715) at the **Abbey of Hautvillers** in Champagne is popularly credited with inventing sparkling Champagne. The historical reality is more complex: Pérignon actually worked hard to *eliminate* bubbles (seen as a wine fault) and was a master blender and cellar manager — his contributions to Champagne's character were real but different. The deliberate production of sparkling wine by a second fermentation is documented in **Limoux** (in Languedoc) at the **Abbaye de Saint-Hilaire** as early as **1531**, predating Pérignon by over a century. **English natural philosopher Christopher Merret** described adding molasses to wine to produce bubbles in a paper read to the Royal Society in **1662**, also before Pérignon.

**Fortified wines** have neutral grape spirit added during or after fermentation to arrest it (if added during) or to preserve and stabilise (if added after):
- **Port**: produced in the **Douro Valley**, Portugal. Spirit added during fermentation (at ~6–8% ABV), killing yeast and preserving residual sugar (~90–120 g/L RS). Aged in **lodges** in **Vila Nova de Gaia** (across the Douro from Porto). Styles: **Vintage Port** (declared years, bottle-aged), **LBV (Late Bottled Vintage)**, **Tawny** (barrel-aged, oxidative, nutty).
- **Sherry**: produced in the **Sherry Triangle** (Jerez de la Frontera, Sanlúcar de Barrameda, El Puerto de Santa María), Spain, from Palomino Fino grapes. Fermented fully dry, then fortified to either ~15% (where **flor** — a yeast veil — grows on the wine's surface, protecting it from oxidation and creating the characteristic fresh, saline Fino and Manzanilla styles) or ~17–18% (where flor cannot survive, producing Oloroso — oxidative, nutty, rich). **Amontillado** begins as Fino and loses its flor, becoming partially oxidised. Aged in a **solera** system — a fractional blending system of multiple vintage years.
- **Madeira**: produced on the Portuguese island of **Madeira**, unique in its **estufagem** (heating) process — wines are deliberately heated in tanks (**estufas**) or in lodges warmed by the sun (**canteiro** method, for finer wines) to simulate a long sea voyage. Grape varieties: **Sercial** (driest), **Verdelho**, **Bual**, **Malmsey** (sweetest). Madeira is virtually indestructible — bottles from the 19th century are still drinking well.

**Blends versus single-varietal wines**: the Bordeaux blend (**Cabernet Sauvignon + Merlot + Cabernet Franc + Petit Verdot + Malbec**) allows each vintage's weather to be compensated — if Cabernet is late-ripening in a cool year, Merlot adds body. The **GSM blend** (Grenache + Syrah + Mourvèdre) is the backbone of Southern Rhône (**Châteauneuf-du-Pape**), Spain's **Priorat**, and Australia's **McLaren Vale**. **Champagne** is typically a blend of Pinot Noir, Chardonnay, and Pinot Meunier — and a blend of multiple vintages in NV — giving the house **chef de cave** (head of cellar) control over a consistent house style. **Krug** and **Bollinger** are famous for their full-scale blending philosophy; **Salon** is famous for its single-year, single-vineyard, single-variety Champagne.

slides.title: Reading a wine list — style, structure, and food pairing logic
slides.body:
A sommelier's practical job includes **reading and designing a wine list**, pairing wine with food, and guiding guests whose budgets, preferences, and palates vary widely. The structural parameters of a wine — **acidity, tannin, sweetness, body, and alcohol** — are the levers that determine food compatibility.

**The classic pairing principles** (articulated by figures including **André Simon**, founder of the Wine and Food Society (1933), and systematised by **Kevin Zraly** in *Windows on the World Complete Wine Course* (1985, now updated annually)) fall into two categories:

- **Congruent pairing**: match like with like — rich wine with rich food; sweet wine with sweet food (the dessert should never be sweeter than the wine); acidic wine with acidic or fatty food (acidity cuts fat — Sancerre with goat's cheese; Champagne with fried food).
- **Contrasting pairing**: bridge differences — salty food with sweet wine (Sauternes with Roquefort, a classic pairing made famous at **Château d'Yquem**); tannic red wine with protein-rich meat (tannin binds salivary proteins, but the proteins in rare steak compete for the tannin, softening its perception).

**Reading grape variety from structure**:
- High tannin + full body + high acid → likely **Nebbiolo** (Barolo/Barbaresco) or **Cabernet Sauvignon** (Médoc, Napa)
- Low tannin + high acid + pale colour → likely **Pinot Noir** (Burgundy) or **Gamay** (Beaujolais — **Georges Duboeuf** is the most famous négociant)
- High acid + aromatic + often off-dry → likely **Riesling** (Mosel, Alsace) or **Gewurztraminer** (Alsace; distinctive lychee / rose / ginger)
- Full body + low acid + earthy + no oak → likely **Grenache**-dominant (Châteauneuf-du-Pape)

**The sommelier's toolbox** for wine list management includes: **bin numbers** (identifying wines quickly without mispronouncing obscure names in front of guests), **vintage charts** (house resources documenting great and poor years by region), **producer notes** (knowing that **Domaine de la Romanée-Conti (DRC)** in Vosne-Romanée makes the world's most expensive Pinot Noir, or that **Château Pétrus** is essentially all Merlot from blue clay), and **decanting protocols** (young tannic reds need air; old Burgundies need gentle handling to avoid disturbing sediment).

**Champagne houses and styles** a sommelier must know:
- **Krug**: full-bodied, complex, multi-vintage Champagne; uses 100% first-press juice fermented in small oak barrels.
- **Bollinger**: Pinot Noir dominant, vinous and structured; produces the single-vineyard **Vieilles Vignes Françaises** from ungrafted pre-phylloxera vines in Aÿ.
- **Louis Roederer**: Cristal (created 1876 for Tsar Alexander II of Russia, who reportedly feared clear bottles concealing bombs — hence crystal-clear glass).
- **Moët & Chandon**: the world's largest Champagne house by volume; **Dom Pérignon** (prestige cuvée) was created in 1936 (vintage 1921).
- **Salon**: single-vintage, single-vineyard (Le Mesnil-sur-Oger, Côte des Blancs), single-variety (Chardonnay) — declared only in exceptional years.

Knowing which style a guest enjoys — creamy autolytic Champagne vs fresh, citrus-led Champagne; tannic structured red vs silky Pinot-driven red — and mapping that to producers, regions, and vintages is the core of advanced sommelier practice.

question.question: Which of the following statements about the méthode traditionnelle for Champagne is accurate?
options: The second fermentation occurs in large stainless-steel tanks; the wine is then transferred to bottles before disgorgement.
Champagne's bubbles result from CO₂ injection at bottling, after which the wine ages on lees for at least 15 months.

In the méthode traditionnelle, a second fermentation occurs in the sealed bottle after addition of the liqueur de tirage; lees aging generates autolytic characters (brioche, biscuit, cream); riddling collects sediment in the neck; disgorgement expels the frozen yeast plug; and dosage adjusts final sweetness — with a minimum of 15 months lees aging for NV Champagne and 36 months for vintage.
Dom Pérignon invented sparkling Champagne in 1668 by sealing bottles with cork before fermentation was complete.
question.explanation: The **méthode traditionnelle** (méthode champenoise) is defined by second fermentation **in the bottle**, not in a tank (that is the **Charmat method** / **cuve close**, used for Prosecco and some Sekt). The sequence is: base wine → **liqueur de tirage** (wine + sugar + yeast) added → crown-capped bottle → **prise de mousse** (second fermentation in bottle, CO₂ dissolves under pressure) → **sur lattes aging** (lees contact: NV minimum 15 months, vintage minimum 36 months per AOC rules — the actual house averages are often much longer) → **remuage/riddling** (manual or gyropalette) → **dégorgement** (neck frozen, crown cap removed, yeast plug expelled) → **dosage** (liqueur d'expédition added) → **cork and cage**. The **Dom Pérignon myth** is historically false: Pérignon worked to eliminate bubbles; sparkling wine is documented in Limoux (1531) and described by Christopher Merret (1662) before Pérignon's work. Option A describes the **Charmat method**. Option D misdates and misattributes the invention.

hints: The key distinction is where the second fermentation happens: bottle vs tank.
What does 'sur lattes' mean, and how long is required for NV Champagne?
slides.workedSolution: The méthode traditionnelle requires second fermentation in the bottle (not tank), a minimum of 15 months lees aging for NV (36 for vintage), riddling to collect sediment, disgorgement to expel it, and dosage to set sweetness level. Dom Pérignon did not invent sparkling wine — that myth is historically false.

question.question: Identify a mystery red wine from structural clues
question.goal: Use tasting descriptors and structure to narrow a red wine to its most likely grape variety and region.

steps.prompt: The wine is pale garnet (almost translucent at the rim), with aromas of dried rose, tar, dried cherry, truffle, and a hint of orange peel. Tannins are very high and grippy; acidity is high; body is medium-full; alcohol ~14%. Which grape variety fits this profile?
steps.motivation: Map aromatic and structural signature to a variety.
hints: Very high tannin + pale colour + rose/tar = one of the great Italian reds.
steps.reveal: **Nebbiolo** is the answer. Its paradoxically pale colour despite very high tannin, combined with the rose/tar/truffle aromatic signature and high acidity, is unique among noble varieties. Its pallor comes from early anthocyanin precipitation — the colour drops out but the tannin (mostly polymeric) remains.

steps.prompt: Which two DOCG appellations in Piedmont, Italy, are made exclusively from Nebbiolo, and what distinguishes them stylistically?
steps.motivation: Locate the variety in its geography.

acceptedAnswers: Barolo and Barbaresco; Barolo is more powerful and requires longer aging; Barbaresco is more elegant and approachable earlier

hints: Both are in the Langhe hills south of the town of Alba.
steps.reveal: **Barolo** (minimum 38 months aging, of which 18 in oak; or 62 months for Riserva) and **Barbaresco** (minimum 26 months, 9 in oak; or 50 for Riserva) are both 100% Nebbiolo DOCGs in Piedmont's Langhe hills. Barolo is generally fuller, more powerful, and longer-lived; Barbaresco (championed by **Angelo Gaja** since the 1960s) is considered more elegant and approachable at an earlier stage.

question.question: Building a Champagne flight for a tasting dinner
question.prompt: A client is hosting a 6-course tasting dinner for 12 guests and wants a Champagne flight of three contrasting styles — one to open the meal with oysters and caviar, one to accompany a mushroom risotto mid-course, and one as a digestif with aged Comté cheese. Drawing on your knowledge of Champagne house styles, grape varieties (Chardonnay, Pinot Noir, Pinot Meunier), lees-aging regimes, dosage levels, and the méthode traditionnelle, propose three specific Champagne styles (you may name houses or generic style descriptors), explain the structural basis for each pairing, and anticipate one question the client might ask about why sparkling wine works with the full range of the menu.

In ≤150 words, explain the Bordeaux blend: which grape varieties it comprises, why blending is used rather than single-varietal wines, and how the blend philosophy differs from the Champagne blending philosophy. Name at least one specific château and one specific Champagne house in your answer.
question.rubric: Should identify Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot, Cabernet Franc, and optionally Petit Verdot and Malbec as the Bordeaux varieties. Should explain that blending compensates for vintage variation — if one variety underperforms in a cool year, another fills the gap. Should contrast Bordeaux (blending varieties from a single vintage across a defined property) with Champagne (blending varieties, parcels, AND multiple vintages to maintain a consistent house style year after year). Should name at least one château (e.g., Château Pétrus, Château Mouton Rothschild, Château Margaux) and one Champagne house (e.g., Krug, Bollinger, Moët & Chandon). Bonus: note that Champagne NV represents the chef de cave's ability to smooth out vintage variation through multi-vintage blending.
